articles.title: What does “as discussed” really mean in your proposal?
articles.intro: You remember the conversation. Your contractor may remember it differently. A written scope gives both of you something clearer to work from.

sections.heading: Turn a conversation into a checklist
sections.text: Look for phrases such as “as discussed,” “standard finish,” or “complete renovation.” Each can stand for several different things. Ask your contractor to describe the work in writing: which rooms, which materials, which quantities, and which installation tasks.

sections.heading: Name what is outside the price
sections.text: Ask whether demolition, removal of debris, patching, painting, fixture installation, and permits are included where relevant to your project. The goal is not to assume these items are missing. It is to replace assumptions with a shared understanding.

sections.heading: A useful question to ask
sections.text: “Can we list the work and materials included in this line item, along with anything I will need to arrange or pay for separately?” Keep the response with the final proposal so you can refer back to the same details.

articles.title: The lowest bid isn’t always the same project.
articles.intro: Two prices are easy to compare. Two scopes take a little more attention. Start by finding out whether the proposals describe the same work.

sections.heading: Compare the ingredients
sections.text: Make a short table with one column for each contractor. Add a row for each part of your project: preparation, materials, installation, finishing, cleanup, and any other work you expect. Record what each proposal actually says. Mark anything missing as a question, rather than guessing.

sections.heading: Put allowances side by side
sections.text: Ask what each allowance is intended to cover. Does it include the product only, or installation too? Which quantities and selections does it assume? Ask how the final price will be adjusted if your selections differ.

sections.heading: Close the gaps before choosing
sections.text: Send each contractor the questions relevant to their proposal. Request written clarifications. Once the scopes are clearer, you can weigh price alongside the work being offered, communication, and the other factors that matter to you.

articles.title: Before you approve that change order, ask these questions.
articles.intro: A change order deserves the same care as the original proposal. Start with the original written scope and follow the change from there.

sections.heading: What exactly has changed?
sections.text: Ask for a description of the added, removed, or revised work. Compare it with the original scope and any previous written changes. Keep the conversation focused on the documents and on what needs to happen next.

sections.heading: What does the new price include?
sections.text: Ask the contractor to identify the labor, materials, and other items covered by the proposed change. If work is being removed, ask whether a credit applies. Clarify any remaining allowances or unknown costs.

sections.heading: What happens to the schedule?
sections.text: Ask whether the change affects the completion date, material lead times, access to your home, or other trades. Request the agreed scope, price adjustment, and schedule impact in writing before making your decision.

before-i-sign.name: Before I Sign
before-i-sign.headline: Know what you’re signing up for.
before-i-sign.description: An experienced second look at a contractor’s proposal before you make a commitment.
items: The written scope and how clearly it describes your project
Allowances and the selections or quantities behind them
Exclusions and responsibilities that may fall to you
Ambiguous language and questions to clarify with your contractor
before-i-sign.send: One proposal or estimate, any written scope, and supporting plans, photos, or notes that help explain the project.

compare-my-bids.name: Compare My Bids
compare-my-bids.eyebrow: TWO OR THREE BIDS. ONE INFORMED DECISION.
compare-my-bids.headline: Compare the project. Then the price.
compare-my-bids.description: Understand how competing proposals line up, where their scopes differ, and what to ask before choosing.
items: Differences in the work described by each contractor
Materials, quantities, and allowances that may explain price differences
Exclusions and items that appear in only some proposals
Questions to bring the proposals onto a more comparable footing
compare-my-bids.send: Two or three proposals for the same project, along with your project description and any shared plans or scope.

change-order-check.name: Change Order Check
change-order-check.headline: Understand what changed. And why it matters.
change-order-check.description: A second opinion on a proposed change order, viewed alongside your original scope.
items: How the proposed change relates to the original written scope
The work being added, removed, or revised
Unclear cost descriptions or schedule implications to clarify
Practical questions to ask before approving the change
change-order-check.send: The original proposal and scope, the proposed change order, previous approved changes, and any relevant photos or correspondence.
